 Q1 (a) Describe the major tasks performed by the front end and back end of a compiler. 5M
 CO-1 · BL-1


A compiler is split into two halves joined by the intermediate representation (IR). The front end (analysis part) depends on the
source language and not on the target machine. The back end (synthesis part) depends on the target machine and not on the
source language.

 Source program → Lexical analyzer → Syntax analyzer → Semantic analyzer → Intermediate code gen. →

 Code optimizer → Code generator → Target code

Blue = front end, green = back end. The symbol table and error handler are shared by all phases.


 Front end (analysis) Back end (synthesis)

 Lexical analysis: reads characters, groups them into lexemes, emits Machine-dependent code optimization: improves IR/target code
 tokens <token-name, attribute> , removes white space (register usage, peephole, use of special instructions).
 and comments.

 Syntax analysis: checks grammar and builds the parse tree / syntax Code generation: instruction selection, register allocation and
 tree. assignment, evaluation order.

 Semantic analysis: type checking, type conversion (coercion), Memory management: maps names to run-time addresses (static,
 scope and declaration checks. stack, heap).

 Intermediate code generation: produces machine-independent IR Produces relocatable machine code or assembly for the target.
 such as three-address code.

 Machine-independent optimization (may be placed in either half), Uses the symbol table to find storage locations and sizes.
 symbol-table creation, error detection and reporting.



 Why split? Retargeting: for m languages and n machines we need only m front ends + n back ends instead of m × n
 complete compilers.



 Q1 (b) Explain the rules to compute CLOSURE() and GOTO() functions in LR parsers. 5M
 CO-1 · BL-2



 An LR(0) item is a production with a dot in its body, e.g. A → X • Y Z . The dot shows how much of the production has
 already been seen on the stack.




Paper 1 · Final Exam 2025-26 CD Solved PYQs · Jay Naik Page 4 of 64

CLOSURE(I)

 1. Every item in I is added to CLOSURE(I).

 2. If A → α • B β is in CLOSURE(I) and B → γ is a production, add B → • γ to CLOSURE(I) (if not already there).

 3. Repeat step 2 until no more new items can be added.

For LR(1) items [A → α • B β, a] , step 2 adds [B → • γ, b] for every terminal b in FIRST(βa).

GOTO(I, X)

GOTO(I, X) = CLOSURE of the set of all items A → α X • β such that A → α • X β is in I. In words: move the dot over X in
every item where X is just after the dot, then take the closure. It gives the DFA transition from state I on grammar symbol X.


 Example (E → E + T | T, T → id). Augment with E' → E.
 I0 = CLOSURE({E' → •E}) = { E' → •E, E → •E+T, E → •T, T → •id }
 GOTO(I0, E) = CLOSURE({E' → E•, E → E•+T}) = { E' → E•, E → E•+T }
 GOTO(I0, id) = { T → id• }

 1. Easy to produce from the source program (by the front end).

 Q2 (A) Illustrate with an example the problem caused by a left-recursive grammar in a recursive descent 10 M
 parser. For the given grammar, eliminate the left recursion.
 G → E E → E + T | T T → E * T | id
 CO-1 · BL-3



1. The problem


 A grammar is left recursive if it has a non-terminal A with a derivation A ⇒+ Aα. It is immediately left recursive if a
 production has the form A → Aα.


A recursive-descent parser has one procedure per non-terminal; the procedure for A picks a production and calls the
procedures of its body from left to right. For E → E + T , procedure E() first calls E() again without consuming any input:

 void E() {
 E(); /* calls itself again, input pointer has not moved */
 match('+');
 T();
 }


Since the lookahead never changes, E() calls E() forever → infinite recursion / stack overflow. Hence top-down parsers
(recursive descent, LL(1)) cannot handle left-recursive grammars, and left recursion must be removed first.

Rule for immediate left recursion: A → Aα1 | … | Aαm | β1 | … | βn becomes
 A → β1A' | … | βnA' A' → α1A' | … | αmA' | ε


2. Spotting the left recursion in the given grammar

 E → E + T is immediate left recursion.

 T → E * T and E → T give T ⇒ E*T ⇒ T*T: this is indirect left recursion through E and T.

So we use the general algorithm: order the non-terminals G, E, T, and for each Ai substitute productions of earlier Aj that start
Ai's bodies, then remove immediate left recursion.


3. Step by step
Step 1 — G: G → E has no left recursion. Unchanged.

Step 2 — E: E → E + T | T. Here α = +T, β = T:

 E → T E'
 E' → + T E' | ε


Step 3 — T: T → E * T starts with E, an earlier non-terminal. Substitute E → T E':

 T → T E' * T | id


Now this is immediate left recursion with α = E' * T and β = id:

 T → id T'
 T' → E' * T T' | ε



 Final grammar without left recursion:
 G→E
 E → T E'
 E' → + T E' | ε
 T → id T'
 T' → E' * T T' | ε


Check: No body now begins with its own head (directly or through other non-terminals): E starts with T, T starts with id, E'
starts with + or ε, T' starts with E' (which starts with +), * or ε. The language is unchanged, e.g. id + id * id : G ⇒ E ⇒ TE'
⇒ id T'E'; T' → E'*TT' with E' → +TE' gives id + id … * id. ✔

1. Common sub-expression elimination (CSE)

An expression E is a common sub-expression if it was computed earlier and none of its operands has changed since. The
second computation is replaced by the earlier result.


 t1 = 4 * i t1 = 4 * i
 x = a[t1] x = a[t1]
 t2 = 4 * i // same as t1 y = b[t1] // t2 removed
 y = b[t2]




2. Copy propagation
After a copy statement x = y , later uses of x are replaced by y (as long as neither changes). This often makes the copy itself
dead.


 x = y x = y // now dead
 z = x + 5 z = y + 5
 w = x * 2 w = y * 2



3. Dead-code elimination

A variable is dead at a point if its value is never used afterwards. Statements that compute only dead values, and unreachable
code, are removed.


 debug = false /* both statements removed */
 if (debug) print(x) // never runs
 a = b + c // a never used




4. Constant folding and constant propagation

Folding: expressions whose operands are constants are evaluated at compile time. Propagation: a variable known to hold a
constant is replaced by that constant.


 pi = 3.14 area = 12.56 // 3.14 * 2 * 2
 r = 2
 area = pi * r * r



(Extra) Loop-related function-preserving techniques

 Code motion: move loop-invariant computation outside the loop: while (i < n-2) → t = n-2; while (i < t) .

 Induction-variable elimination & strength reduction: replace t = 4*i inside the loop with t = t + 4 (multiplication →
 addition).

 Q4 (A) What are top-down parsers? Write the algorithm for constructing the predictive parsing table. 10 M
 CO-1 · BL-2



 Top-down parsing builds the parse tree from the root (start symbol) down to the leaves, in preorder. It finds a leftmost
 derivation of the input.


Types: (1) Recursive descent with backtracking: tries productions one by one and backtracks on failure; (2) Predictive parsing
(no backtracking): recursive predictive parser or table-driven LL(1) parser. The production is chosen using one lookahead
symbol. Grammar must be free of left recursion and left-factored.

LL(1): scan input Left to right, produce a Leftmost derivation, use 1 lookahead symbol. Model: input buffer, stack (starts with
$S ), parsing table M[A, a], output.


FIRST and FOLLOW (needed for the table)
 FIRST(α): set of terminals that begin strings derived from α (plus ε if α ⇒* ε). If X is a terminal, FIRST(X) = {X}; for X → Y1Y2…,
 add FIRST(Y1) − {ε}, and if Y1 ⇒* ε continue with Y2, etc.

 FOLLOW(A): terminals that can appear immediately to the right of A. Put $ in FOLLOW(S); for B → αAβ add FIRST(β) − {ε};
 for B → αA, or B → αAβ with ε ∈ FIRST(β), add FOLLOW(B).

Algorithm: construction of predictive parsing table M


 Input: grammar G. Output: parsing table M.
 Method: for each production A → α of the grammar:

 1. For each terminal a in FIRST(α), add A → α to M[A, a].

 2. If ε is in FIRST(α), then for each terminal b in FOLLOW(A), add A → α to M[A, b].

 3. If ε is in FIRST(α) and $ is in FOLLOW(A), add A → α to M[A, $].

 After all productions: every undefined entry of M is error. If any entry has more than one production, the grammar is not
 LL(1).


Predictive parsing (driver) algorithm

 push $ ; push S ; a = first input symbol
 while (X = top) != $ :
 if X == a : pop; a = next symbol /* match */
 else if X is terminal: error()
 else if M[X,a] empty : error()
 else if M[X,a] = X → Y1 Y2 … Yk :
 output the production; pop X;
 push Yk … Y2 Y1 (Y1 on top)
 accept when X == $ and a == $



 Mini example: E → TE', E' → +TE' | ε, T → id. FIRST(TE') = {id} → M[E,id] = E→TE'; FIRST(+TE') = {+} → M[E',+]; E'→ε goes
 under FOLLOW(E') = {$} → M[E',$]; M[T,id] = T→id. No multiple entries → LL(1).

(i) Static allocation

 Storage for all data objects is laid out at compile time. Names are bound to storage once, and the binding does not change
 at run time.

 Used for global variables, static locals and constants. FORTRAN-77 used it for everything.

 Pros: no run-time allocation overhead, addresses known at compile time, values persist between calls.

 Cons: size of every object must be known at compile time; no recursion (only one activation record per procedure); no

(ii) Stack allocation
 Storage is organized as a stack of activation records. An AR is pushed when a procedure is called and popped when it
 returns.

 Locals are bound to fresh storage in each activation, so recursion is supported. Locals are reached at fixed offsets from the
 stack/frame pointer.

 Used for local variables, parameters and return addresses in C, C++, Java, Pascal.

 Cons: values of locals are lost when the activation ends; dangling references if a pointer to a local outlives its activation;
 sizes of locals must be fixed (or known at call time).

 Call sequence: SP = SP + caller.recordsize; *SP = here + 16 (return address); goto callee
 Return: SP = SP - caller.recordsize; goto *0(SP)


(iii) Heap allocation

 Storage is allocated and freed in any order at run time from a large pool (the heap), e.g. malloc/free , new/delete ,

 closures).

 Managed by a memory manager: keeps free lists, uses first-fit/best-fit, coalesces adjacent free blocks. Deallocation can be
